intro:
By the end of this track you can design a company's data as one system of record plus derived views, and keep the whole thing correct without distributed transactions. You'll trace every store back to the log that feeds it and know where a single total order stops, change a derived table's shape by replaying the log into a second version, build indexes, views and client pushes as consumers of one write path, and carry one operation ID from the phone to a unique constraint so retries never move money twice. Then you'll enforce rules such as unique handles through a partitioned log, separate timeliness from integrity, audit derived data with recomputation, Merkle trees and hash chains, and design for the people the data describes: bias in automated decisions, privacy, consent, the law as of November 2026, and erasure in systems built never to forget.

This is the last track, and it leans on the whole course. You'll get the most from it after Messaging and logs (partitions, keys, offsets, compaction), Stream processing (change data capture, event sourcing, state and exactly-once), Transactions (write skew, two-phase commit, sagas) and Consistency and consensus (total order broadcast). Each lesson points back to the one it builds on instead of teaching it again.

The labs are plain Kotlin in the `sim` module, one package per lesson (`sfz.derive.l01` to `sfz.derive.l06`), and need no Docker. They model logs, processors, crashes and retries in memory on a seeded, deterministic scheduler or in virtual time, so a month of payments, a thousand crashes or a race between 64 clients runs in about a second and gives the same counts on every laptop. Lesson 6's lab uses the JDK's own `javax.crypto` for AES-GCM. From the `labs` folder, run `./gradlew :sim:test --tests 'sfz.derive.lNN.*'` until it passes; `./gradlew :sim:solutionTest --tests 'sfz.derive.lNN.*'` runs the same tests against the reference answers, and the Try its run demos with `./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=<class> --console=plain -q`.
cheatsheet:
## Words this track defines

| Term | Meaning | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| System of record | where a fact is written first; wins every disagreement | 1 |
| Derived data | written only from the system of record's log, so it can be dropped and rebuilt | 1 |
| Total order | one sequence for all events; one log partition gives one, one leader caps it | 1 |
| Lambda, kappa | batch plus speed layer merged at read time; one stream job replayed from a retained log | 1 |
| Reprocessing | new code over old input into a second version, readers moved over gradually | 1 |
| Unbundling, federation | one write log feeding separate stores; one query over stores as they are | 2 |
| Write path, read path | work done when data arrives; work done when someone asks | 2 |
| End-to-end argument | duplicate suppression, integrity and encryption are complete only at the endpoints | 3 |
| Operation (request) ID | one ID per user intent, made by the client, carried to a unique constraint at the final write | 3 |
| Dedupe window | how long IDs are remembered; a later retry counts as new | 3 |
| Partition key | decides which partition, and so which single decider, sees a record | 4 |
| Timeliness, integrity | up-to-date reads (violations heal); nothing lost, invented or contradictory (violations stay) | 4 |
| Invariant confluence | a rule replicas can each keep alone and still keep after merging | 4 |
| Compensating action | the apology that repairs a rule checked late: refund, voucher, rebooking | 4 |
| Audit, reconciliation | recompute a view and diff it per key; compare totals (an alarm, not an audit) | 5 |
| Merkle tree, hash chain | hashes over key ranges for cheap comparison; each entry hashing its predecessor | 5 |
| Transparency log, data contract | a publicly checkable Merkle log; a machine-checked promise about a dataset | 5 |
| Proxy variable, feedback loop | an input that stands in for a protected group; decisions changing tomorrow's training data | 6 |
| Crypto-shredding, erasure ledger | erase by destroying a per-person key; a record of erasures applied again on every restore | 6 |

## Patterns

| Problem | Pattern | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Keep a search index, cache and warehouse in step with the database | CDC or an outbox into one log; every store is a consumer | 1, 2 |
| Change a derived table's shape | second job from offset 0 into v2, shift readers by a hash of their ID, keep v1 until 100% | 1 |
| A replay puts a month into today | window by event time, never processing time | 1 |
| A user can't see their own write in the view | the write returns its offset; the read waits until the view has applied it | 2 |
| A retried request moves money twice | operation ID from the client, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` in the same transaction as the effect | 3 |
| Enforce a unique value at scale | key the log by that value; one single-threaded processor per partition decides in order | 4 |
| Move money between partitions without 2PC | append one request; the source processor debits and emits a credit with the same ID; the destination drops duplicates | 4 |
| A rule that can be broken briefly | check late, repair with a compensating action; check synchronously before anything irreversible | 4 |
| Find drift in a derived view | replay the log into a fresh view and diff per key; a Merkle tree when the views live apart | 5 |
| Prove history wasn't rewritten | hash chain, with its head published where the owner can't change it | 5 |
| Bad data from another team | data quality checks and a data contract, run by both sides; stop the line on failure | 5 |
| Erase a person from logs you can't edit | per-person keys (crypto-shredding), personal data out of events, bounded compaction, snapshot expiry, an erasure ledger | 6 |

## Questions to ask of any dataflow

1. Which store is the system of record for each fact, and what feeds every other copy? Could you drop and rebuild each one?
2. Where does the total order stop, and which rules relate records that no single partition sees?
3. Which ID makes a retry harmless, who creates it, and where is it enforced? How long is it remembered?
4. For each rule: does it need one decider (a unique index, one partition), or can it be checked late and repaired?
5. Which reads need their own write, and how do they wait for it?
6. What recomputes each view and compares it, and who holds the head of the audit log?
7. For each automated decision: what is recorded, who can overturn it, and are error rates measured per group?
8. For each copy of a person's data: how does a deletion reach it, how long does it take, and what happens on restore?

## How the whole course fits together

The course started with one picture: a system of record and data derived from it, judged by its latency percentiles, its faults and its load. The networking and operating-systems tracks showed the machinery every number rests on. On one machine, the data models, storage engines, caches and encodings turned records into bytes, indexes and views that a single server can find fast and keep after a crash. Across machines, replication made copies, partitioning split them, transactions kept concurrent writers from breaking rules, the faults, time and truth track showed what goes wrong when networks, clocks and processes misbehave, and consensus let machines agree on one order anyway. The last part moved data between systems: logs gave every consumer the same order, stream and batch processing derived new data from it, and this track joined it all into one design, a log as the system of record and everything else derived, kept correct end to end by operation IDs, single deciders, audits and the care owed to the people the records describe.
recap: Name one system of record per fact and feed every other store from its log, by CDC or an outbox. A derived store is written only from that log, so it can be dropped and rebuilt.
A single total order stops at one leader's throughput, at regions, at service boundaries and at offline clients; past that, order per key and carry causal links in the data.

Change a derived table's shape by replaying the retained log into a second version with event-time windows, moving a stable share of readers over, and keeping the old version until the last reader leaves.

Indexes, replicas and views are all snapshot, catch up, keep up. Unbundling runs that machinery as consumers of one write log; streaming databases maintain the views for you and are still behind, so a read that needs its own write waits for its offset.

Exactly-once inside one layer stops at that layer's edge. One operation ID per user intent, made by the client and enforced by a unique constraint with the effect, is the only thing that takes duplicates to zero.

Uniqueness needs one decider per value: key the log by the constrained value. A transfer across partitions is one appended request plus derived debits and credits, deduplicated by ID, with no distributed transaction.

Timeliness violations heal by waiting; integrity violations stay. Guarantee integrity everywhere, buy timeliness where users need it, and check late with apologies wherever a rule is invariant confluent or the apology is cheap.

Hardware, databases and your own code corrupt data silently. Recompute derived views and diff them, compare far-apart views with Merkle trees, hash-chain the log and publish its head, and check data where it crosses team boundaries.

Automated decisions repeat the bias in their data through proxies and feedback loops; record each decision's inputs and reasons, measure errors per group, and keep a human who can overturn it. Personal data is a liability: collect less and keep it for a stated time.

Erasure must reach every copy: topics, compaction, snapshots, derived views and backups. Crypto-shredding makes copies you can't edit unreadable, every restore must re-apply the erasure record, and the legal status of key destruction is still open. None of this is legal advice.

quiz.q: The team wants to change a derived revenue table from per-day to per-merchant-per-hour, with no downtime and a way back. What do you do?
options: Migrate the table in place over a weekend with an ALTER and an UPDATE
Run a second copy of the job from offset 0 into a new table, move readers over gradually, and retire the old table only at 100%
Add the new columns to the speed layer and merge them with the batch layer at read time
Write the new shape from the application in parallel with the old one
quiz.why: That is Kreps's reprocessing recipe: the log is retained, so a second job can build v2 next to v1, readers move over a stable share at a time, and v1 stays as the way back until it is retired. Writing both shapes from the application is a dual write, and an in-place migration has no rollback.

quiz.q: A replayed stream job puts a whole month of payments into today's revenue window. What went wrong?
options: The log's retention was too short
The job ran with exactly-once disabled
The job windows by processing time, which during a replay is now for every record
The partitions were read out of order
quiz.why: During a replay every record is processed now, so processing-time windows put everything in the window that holds the replay's own time. Windowing by the event time inside each record puts each payment on the day it happened.

quiz.q: A user changes their payout account, and the settings page, which reads a streaming database's view, still shows the old one. Which fix keeps the view as the read path?
options: Poll the view faster
Write to the view directly from the API
Return the write's log offset and have the read wait until the view has applied it
Cache the old value for a shorter time
quiz.why: The view is derived and always somewhat behind. Waiting for the write's own offset (or LSN) gives read-your-writes for the reads that need it and costs nothing for the others. Faster polling shrinks the window without closing it, and writing to the view directly makes it a second system of record.

quiz.q: A pipeline has TCP, Kafka's idempotent producer and Kafka exactly-once processing, and still writes duplicate ledger rows when a phone retries a transfer. What fixes it?
options: An operation ID made on the phone, carried through every hop, and enforced by a unique constraint in the same transaction as the ledger write
Turning on exactly-once in the consumer as well
Longer timeouts on the phone so it retries less
A SELECT for an existing row before the INSERT
quiz.why: Each layer deduplicates only its own retries, and the phone's retry is a new request to all of them. Only an ID for the user's intent, checked at the final effect, recognises it. A SELECT before the INSERT is check-then-insert and fails at read committed; longer timeouts make duplicates rarer, not impossible.

quiz.q: Unique idempotency keys per merchant are enforced by a stream processor. Which partition key makes that correct?
options: Payment ID
Customer ID
Merchant ID and idempotency key
A random key, for even load
quiz.why: Every request that could conflict must reach the same single decider, so the key must be exactly the value the rule is about. Keyed by payment or customer ID, two requests with the same idempotency key can land in two partitions, and both are accepted.

quiz.q: Which of these needs coordination (one decider), rather than a check after the fact?
options: Every payment amount is positive
Every new refund references an existing payment
A wallet's balance never goes below zero
Payout IDs are unique, generated by each region from its own range
quiz.why: A balance with a lower bound under withdrawals is not invariant confluent: two regions can each spend the last 50.00. Value checks, foreign-key inserts and IDs from separate ranges merge safely. A business may still choose to check the balance late and repair it with an overdraft fee, which is an apology by design.

quiz.q: An hourly reconciliation shows the sum of balances equals the sum of postings, yet the hourly per-account audit finds two accounts wrong. How can both be true?
options: The audit has a bug: if the totals match, every account matches
Two errors of opposite sign cancel in the total but not per account
The reconciliation ran before the audit
The Merkle tree hashed the wrong ranges
quiz.why: A total is one number, so +16 in one account and -16 in another leave it unchanged. That is why sums and counts are alarms and only the key-by-key recompute is an audit.

quiz.q: An insider rewrites one old ledger entry and recomputes every later hash in the chain. What still catches it?
options: Verifying the chain from the first entry
The CRC of the rewritten record
The head hash the auditors received before the rewrite
Nothing
quiz.why: A fully recomputed chain is consistent with itself, and a CRC is as easy to recompute as a hash. A head held by someone the insider can't reach no longer matches. Transparency logs such as Certificate Transparency rely on the same idea, with monitors keeping the tree heads they have seen.

quiz.q: A fraud model never reads the customer's group, yet blocks honest customers in one neighbourhood three times as often as elsewhere. What is the most likely mechanism, and the first thing to do?
options: Random noise; retrain with a new seed
A proxy, such as a postcode score learned from biased past investigations; measure error rates per group and test the model without the proxy
Too little training data; collect more of the same labels
The threshold is too high; lower it for everyone
quiz.why: Inputs that correlate with the group carry the bias of the records they were learned from, and more of the same labels repeats it. Measuring false-positive rates per group finds it, and a model without the proxy can often catch about as much fraud with even error rates, as the lesson 6 demo showed.

quiz.q: Personal fields in an event log are encrypted with a key per customer, and a customer has been erased by deleting their key. Which event brings their data back?
options: Replaying the event log from offset 0
Compacting the topic
Expiring old Iceberg snapshots
Restoring the key store from a backup taken before the erasure, without re-applying the erasure record
quiz.why: A replay with the key gone shows the customer as erased, and compaction or snapshot expiry only remove more. An old key backup holds the deleted key, so a restore makes every event readable again unless it forgets everyone in the erasure ledger afterwards, which is what the EDPB asks for backups that can't be edited.
